results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec
All 41 aligned units summarise to the controlling idea of their spec paragraph (p01-p41); the three intro callouts carry the roadmap, the thesis (KEY POINTS) and the failure patterns.

Two units marked two_ideas: Before the Sale ¶2 (two quiet failures of the step-1 hand-off) and Had the Balance Been Empty ¶3 (Adyen's 30-day rule and the Managed Risk pilot). In both the spec's controlling idea itself is one claim with two instances ('fails quietly, in two ways'; 'what Adyen documents about the shortfall'), so neither is two separate controlling ideas.
Every body unit traces to S1-S5: step 1 and the split to S1, the fee to S2, claim/payout/refund to S3, refund debit and shortfall to S4, ledger, step table and decisions to S5.

results.spec_locus: /sections/5/paragraphs/1 (evidence: table 'who is short and who stands behind')
results.quote: Stripe thus publishes an order of collection and a number of days.
results.finding: The shortfall table is followed by Figure 3 and then a sentence that refers back past the table to the Stripe prose; no sentence says what the table shows. Worse, its destination-charge row ('The refund waits as `pending` for up to 45 days') describes the platform's own balance being short, while the prose just above says the destination-charge problem is the reversal error against the studio's short balance, so the table reads as contradicting the paragraph it belongs to. Add a sentence after the table stating what it answers and align the destination-charge row with the prose (or say which balance each column means).

Other evidence passes: Figures 1-3 have captions stating what they show; the step table is followed by 'Read down the last column'; the decisions table by 'Left undecided...'; the ledger table is explained by 'The last row is the counterfactual' and 'The sixth row is the entry...'; the fee table by the 'matter of time' paragraph; the split and refund tables restate the instruction just described; every quotation is followed or framed by what it shows.

All declared transition_in relationships are expressed at their boundaries (e.g. 'The answer has three parts.' problem_solution; 'The hand-off from this state to a payment fails quietly' contrast; 'The hand-off from payment to cost is therefore a matter of time' cause_effect; 'Every one of those routes needs a studio that still sells... so Larkfield keeps a figure' problem_solution; 'Mila's €84.00 went back because she asked... There the money goes back because the cardholder's bank says so' contrast). The 'Stripe thus... Adyen publishes a shorter period' contrast is present but displaced by the table and figure; recorded under flow_is_followable.

Both readers describe the organising principle as chronological along one payment, framed question -> walk -> synthesis/decisions, with Adyen-vs-Stripe comparison inside each step: this agrees with the declared chronological + problem_solution + comparison pattern. Neither reader marked any section's position unclear. Lost-thread points judged material are recorded as separate fails below; minor points not failed: 'those two rows' back-reference (both readers, understood), K3/Keel (glossed inline), chargeback aside in the split paragraph and the chargeback switch in the Stripe shortfall paragraph (spec-mandated content), dense step-10 paragraph ('followable but heavy').

results.draft_locus: Had the Balance Been Empty ¶2 (table, row 'Stripe, destination charge')
results.quote: the refund request returns an error instead of creating a refund with `pending` status.
results.finding: Both readers found the destination-charge row contradicting the preceding prose (reversal returns an error instead of a pending refund) and had to re-read both to work out which balance each refers to. The table row (not in units.json) reads: 'Stripe, destination charge | The platform's balance | The refund waits as `pending` for up to 45 days | Nobody: the platform has paid, and must reverse the transfer to recover'.

results.quote: Stripe thus publishes an order of collection and a number of days.
results.finding: 'Thus' points back over a table and Figure 3 to the Stripe paragraph, so the Stripe-Adyen contrast is separated from what it compares and the Adyen material appears split. The spec order (Stripe, then Adyen's period and pilot) is fine; place the table and figure after this paragraph or restate the Stripe side.

results.quote: for platforms outside the pilot, Adyen's split-refund page describes the earlier logic only for refunds of the full amount.
results.finding: Both readers read the bare-refund paragraph twice: nested qualifiers (pilot, store profile, platform default, capture glossed in passing, whole vs partial capture) bury the point, and the closing clause leaves the outcome of a bare partial refund outside the pilot unclear. Split the default from the pilot caveat and say plainly what is and is not documented for a partial refund outside the pilot.

results.quote: The sixth row is the entry Larkfield did not have in 2025.
results.finding: The ledger table puts the 25 March 'Payout marked arrived' row before the two 18 March refund rows in an otherwise chronological chapter, and 'the sixth row' comes a paragraph later, so both readers stopped to check dates and count rows. Sort the rows by date or number them, and name the row ('the refund row') instead of its position.
The section announces two steps but never marks where step 3 (the platform's fee) begins; both readers had to wait for the step table to learn what step 3 is.

results.quote: Second, the instruction that divides a payment, the split of the next step, names the studio's account at the provider
results.finding: The second quiet failure uses split, balance account and liable balance account before the next section explains them; one reader had to read on and come back. The spec places this failure in step 1, so the fix is in the prose: a short gloss of the liable balance account here, or a pointer forward.

results.quote: by my arithmetic €84.00 is 70% of €120.00, so 70% of the €120.00 transferred is reversed, which is €84.00.
results.finding: Both readers paused: the sentence reads as circular and leaves open whether €120.00 or €117.47 was transferred. Remind the reader that a destination charge transfers the full €120.00 and the fee comes back separately.

results.quote: The steps showed it three times: Adyen books a split amount with no account, the fees of step 4 and, under its pilot logic, the bare partial refund of step 7 to the liable balance account, and Stripe leaves the transferred funds with the studio and debits the platform.
results.finding: 'Three times' is followed by four cases (three Adyen, one Stripe); the reader could not tell which three were meant.

results.quote: Stripe's Refund object has a status, and a refund against a short balance stays `pending` and "fails with a `failure_reason` of `insufficient_funds`" after 45 days.
results.finding: A short-balance case appears in step 8, where the balance covers the refund, and on destination charges it is unclear which balance would be short. The spec's evidence for p24 includes this quote, so say whose balance (the platform's, or the studio's on a direct charge).

Terms on the audience's does_not_know list that appear are explained at first use (issuer = 'Mila's bank', chargeback = 'a reversal forced by the cardholder's bank', dispute window, scheme = card network, capture, payout, capability, SEPA); other platform terms (split, balance account, connected account, destination charge, balance transaction) are glossed and are covered by earlier chapters of the book.

results.quote: At Larkfield's assumed blended rate it would be €0.87.
results.finding: 'Blended rate' is not explained, nor why the Stripe cost differs from Adyen's €0.61; one flow reader re-read looking for a definition. Minor: a clause ('one average rate across card types') would do.

The introduction opens on a dated, puzzling scenario ending in a question, with a bridge to earlier journeys and an explicit thesis; no weak pattern (no dictionary definition, no 'in today's world', no announcement-only opening).

The conclusion sorts findings by how settled they are, states the author's position, gives questions and hands off to the dispute journey by contrast; it does not merely restate the introduction or end on a generic call to action.

'The account model is the answer to "who pays" for every later refund... I decide it as a liability question, first, and store it per studio and provider' synthesises the walk and states what follows; the Questions turn it into a course of action. (The spec's so_what contrast with the €317,200 of 2025 is not repeated in the conclusion, but it is stated in the ledger section; not failed.)

'Aylin's question had one answer only once the payment was walked through every hand-off. Product, finance and the CTO each knew a step; the €84.00 came from other members' payments in Studio Noord's balance account, with Larkfield's liable balance account behind them.' answers the hook's question and the three answers of the scene.

The cold reader predicted all nine roadmap promises in the right order (question at Larkfield, state before sale, split of 9 March with later cost, claim and payout, refund of 18 March, counterfactual shortfall, ledger entries, step table, four decisions). Its uncertainties (whether the shortfall is counterfactual; how steps map to sections) do not contradict the roadmap and are resolved in the body.

The cold reader gave every element of the expected answer: on Adyen the refund is deducted only from balance accounts the payment credited, the tutor's account goes negative with the liable balance account behind it, 30 days then the reserved compensation account, Managed Risk as a pilot exception; recovery by top-up/direct debit needing a prior SEPA mandate. On Stripe destination charges debit the platform and the reversal errors on a short tutor balance; direct charges hold the refund pending and fail after 45 days. Beforehand: refund split, fee, consent to debit, per-seller exposure figure and a 'to recover from' ledger entry. Its open points (full vs partial, outcome for the parent after 45 days) go beyond the expected answer.

The cold reader explained that Adyen calculates transaction fees after the request so the split can name who bears each fee type but not the amount, that with no instruction Adyen adds a PaymentFee split to the liable balance account, that on Stripe the payer follows from charge type and fee configuration and the amount is read from the balance transaction, and that the ledger records the fee at payment and the cost when reported, reconciled later. Matches expected.

results.quote: The pairing of the two vocabularies is this book's own mapping and an inference: neither company publishes a translation into the other's terms.
results.finding: The mapping disclaimer is stated once (Introduction ¶5). Each step names the Adyen resource and its Stripe counterpart (capabilities allowed/enabled vs active; splits items vs destination charge and application_fee_amount; fee split types vs charge type/fee configuration and balance transaction; settlement delay vs Dutch schedule; payout booked vs paid; refund splits vs reverse_transfer/refund_application_fee; REFUND webhook vs Refund object; liable balance account and 30 days vs loss responsibility and 180-day reserve; top-up/internal transfer vs offsetting/account debit/transfer reversal; accounting report vs balance transactions), and the step table repeats both per row. Small gap, not failed: in 9 March ¶2 the confirming records for the split (transfer webhooks, Balance Platform Accounting Report) are Adyen-only; the Stripe counterpart appears only generically in the step-table paragraph ('an object with a status that can be read again') and in step 11 (balance transactions).
